Assigning samples to treatment groups

Source: vignettes/includeMetadata.Rmd
includeMetadata.Rmd
library(rscprep)
library(Seurat)

Treatment group, genotype, timepoint – the things you actually want to compare – have to get attached to the objects somewhere. includeMetadata() does that from a sample-level table, keyed on the names of the list seuratFrom10x() returns.

Why not just put it in the manifest?

Because the manifest is a different kind of table. Its rows are Cell Ranger runs – one per outs/ directory. Treatment is a property of a sample. For a plain cellranger count run those happen to coincide, so it is tempting to add a Treatment column and be done:

manifest <- data.frame(
  Path        = "/path/to/Sample_1/outs",
  multi = FALSE,
  Treatment   = "Control"     # works here, and only here
)

But a multiplexed run breaks it. One row of the manifest, one outs/ directory, and eight demuxed samples inside it – possibly four controls and four treated. There is no way to write four values in one cell that isn’t a delimited string you then have to parse and validate.

So the two tables stay separate, at their own grain:

  • manifest – run-level: Path, multi, and legitimately things like Batch or RunDate that really do apply to the whole run.
  • sample sheet – sample-level: one row per sample, however many runs they came from.

By the time seuratFrom10x() hands you a list, every entry is one sample and the multiplexed/non-multiplexed distinction has been erased. That is the right moment to attach sample-level metadata, and it is the same code path either way.

The workflow 

seurat_list <- seuratFrom10x(
  path        = "/path/to/Pool1/outs",
  multi = TRUE
)

names(seurat_list)
#> [1] "Bleo_18_Slim_10" "Bleo_22_Slim_14" "Ctrl_04_Slim_02" "Ctrl_09_Slim_07"

Those names are what you key on. Write a sheet against them:

sheet <- data.frame(
  Sample    = c("Bleo_18_Slim_10", "Bleo_22_Slim_14",
                "Ctrl_04_Slim_02", "Ctrl_09_Slim_07"),
  Treatment = c("Bleomycin", "Bleomycin", "Control", "Control"),
  Timepoint = c("D21", "D21", "D21", "D21")
)

annotated <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, sheet)
#> ✔ Added 2 metadata columns to 4 objects: "Treatment" and "Timepoint"

In practice the sheet lives in a CSV next to your analysis, filled in by whoever ran the experiment and kept under version control:

sheet     <- read.csv("samplesheet.csv")
annotated <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, sheet)

Each column is broadcast across every cell of its sample, so after merging you can group by it directly:

merged <- mergeSeurat(annotated)

table(merged$Ident, merged$Treatment)

You don’t have to know the sample names in advance – per_sample_outs/ does. Load first, read names(seurat_list), and write the sheet against what is actually there. Discovery is automatic; the assignment stays explicit.

Identifying samples by rownames

A Sample column is the primary key because it survives a CSV round trip. Rownames work too, and are used whenever there is no Sample column:

sheet <- data.frame(Treatment = c("Control", "Bleomycin"))
rownames(sheet) <- c("Sample_A", "Sample_B")

annotated <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, sheet)

If both are present the column wins. A data frame with neither – so, default 1, 2, 3 rownames – is rejected rather than matched positionally, because lining rows up by position against a list whose order you did not choose is a silent way to mislabel an entire experiment.

Every column, every sample

The rule includeMetadata() enforces is that a column, once present, is populated for all samples. A sample with no row is an error. So is an NA, an empty cell, or a whitespace-only cell:

sheet <- data.frame(
  Sample    = c("Sample_A", "Sample_B", "Sample_C"),
  Treatment = c("Control", NA, "Bleomycin"),
  Timepoint = c(NA, "D21", "")
)

includeMetadata(seurat_list, sheet)
#> Error:
#> Every column of `metadata` must be populated for every sample.
#> ✖ Treatment: missing for "Sample_B"
#> ✖ Timepoint: missing for "Sample_A" and "Sample_C"
#> ℹ A column left blank for some samples becomes `NA` for their cells after
#>   `mergeSeurat()`.

Every offending column is reported at once, so a forty-sample sheet gets fixed in one pass rather than forty.

This strictness exists because the alternative is silent. Seurat::merge() will happily combine an object carrying a Treatment column with one that doesn’t – it fills the gap with NA and says nothing:

annotated   <- seurat_list$Sample_A
unannotated <- seurat_list$Sample_B
annotated$Treatment <- "Control"

merged <- merge(annotated, unannotated, add.cell.id = c("Sample_A", "Sample_B"))

table(merged$Treatment, useNA = "ifany")
#> Control    <NA>
#>    4821    5104

Those NA cells then quietly drop out of every grouped comparison downstream. By the time you notice a group is short, the cause is several steps back. Requiring completeness up front makes the state unreachable.

Master sheets

Rows that match no loaded object are ignored with a warning, so one sheet can describe a whole experiment while you work on a subset:

# sheet covers all 40 samples; only Pool1's 4 are loaded
annotated <- includeMetadata(seurat_list, master_sheet)
#> ! Ignoring 36 rows of `metadata` matching no object in `objList`: ...
#> ✔ Added 2 metadata columns to 4 objects: "Treatment" and "Timepoint"

A typo is still caught, because a mistyped name in the sheet leaves some object without a row – and that is a hard error, not a warning.

Two smaller rules

Existing columns are protected. Re-running against an edited sheet errors unless you opt in:

includeMetadata(annotated, corrected_sheet, overwrite = TRUE)

Ident is reserved and cannot be set at all, even with overwrite = TRUE – it identifies the sample of origin and is what mergeSeurat() verifies after merging.

Column names must be syntactically valid. Seurat quietly runs make.names() on metadata column names, so Cell Type would land as Cell.Type and stop matching the header in your sheet. includeMetadata() refuses instead, and tells you what the name would have become. Note that read.csv() already does this conversion for you by default, so it rarely comes up.

A note on factors

Column types are preserved, factors included – each object keeps the sheet’s full level set, not just the level it happens to carry, so per-sample subsets stay comparable.

That survives on the list but not through a merge: Seurat::merge() flattens factors to character. If you want an ordered factor on the merged object, re-apply it afterwards:

merged <- mergeSeurat(annotated)
merged$Treatment <- factor(merged$Treatment, levels = c("Control", "Bleomycin"))
